paper_title: Questioning the Questions: Sustaining Self-Evolution in Reasoning Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Self-evolving reasoning models learn from their own generated questions, yet repeated self-training can lead to performance collapse. In this paper, we investigate why performance deteriorates over successive rounds and how to sustain self-evolution. Our analysis identifies two recurring quality problems in self-generated questions: invalid questions and repeated variants of the same mathematical questions. First, invalid questions become more prevalent across rounds, and answer-consistency filtering further increases their proportion in training data. Second, existing question diversity controls based on lexical similarity can miss mathematically equivalent questions expressed in different ways, which leads to question diversity collapse in later training rounds. Building on these findings, we introduce R-Quest, which uses question validity and novelty feedback to guide self-evolution. We first train the solver to recognize and reject invalid questions, then use its judgments to guide questioner rewards and filter solver training data. To avoid question repetition, we use a frozen base model to compare sampled question pairs and provide novelty feedback. Empirically, our method consistently achieves the highest average performance on 12 benchmarks in mathematical reasoning, general-domain reasoning, and code generation across two model families. Additionally, R-Quest maintains stable performance gains over ten rounds of self-evolution, peaking in the final round and outperforming R-Zero by 17.32 points.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Self-evolving reasoning models learn from their own generated questions, yet repeated self-training can lead to performance collapse. In this paper, we investigate why performance deteriorates over successive rounds and how to sustain self-evolution. Our analysis identifies two recurring quality problems in selfgenerated questions: invalid questions and repeated variants of the same mathematical questions. First, invalid questions become more prevalent across rounds, and answer-consistency filtering further increases their proportion in training data. Second, existing question diversity controls based on lexical similarity can miss mathematically equivalent questions expressed in different ways, which leads to question diversity collapse in later training rounds. Building on these findings, we introduce R-Quest, which uses question validity and novelty feedback to guide self-evolution. We first train the solver to recognize and reject invalid questions, then use its judgments to guide questioner rewards and filter solver training data. To avoid question repetition, we use frozen base model to compare sampled question pairs and provide novelty feedback. Empirically, our method consistently achieves the highest average performance on 12 benchmarks in mathematical reasoning, general-domain reasoning, and code generation across two model families. Additionally, R-Quest maintains stable performance gains over ten rounds of selfevolution, peaking in the final round and outperforming R-Zero by 17.32 points.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Self-evolving reasoning models learn by generating and solving their own training tasks (Huang et al., 2026a; 2023; Tao et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2026), reducing their dependence on humancurated data. Recent frameworks organize this process around questioner and solver roles: the questioner learns to propose challenging problems, while the solver learns to solve them, allowing both roles to co-evolve through reinforcement learning (Zhao et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026). However, continued self-evolution can reverse early gains and ultimately lead to performance collapse (Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). In this paper, we study the practical bottlenecks to sustained self-evolution: Why does performance deteriorate over successive rounds, and how can we address these bottlenecks to achieve sustained self-improvement? To understand why these gains fail to persist, we examine the self-generated questions by R-Zero (Huang et al., Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Average performance on seven math benchmarks. R-Quest exceeds the peak of R-Zero in every round and peaks at round ten, leading by 17.32 points.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 2: Two question-quality problems in self-evolution and how R-Quest addresses them: (a) R-Quest can recognize and reject invalid questions; (b) R-Quest can detect repeated mathematical tasks despite differences in expression. 2025). Our analysis reveals two recurring quality issues: (1) invalid questions and (2) repeated variants of the same mathematical tasks. First, some generated questions are invalid (e.g., due to ambiguous definitions, missing conditions or contradictory assumptions), yet the solver is not explicitly trained to reject such questions, as shown in Figure 2(a). The loop therefore lacks mechanism to exclude or suppress invalid questions. We find that invalid questions become more prevalent across rounds and that answer-consistency filtering further increases their proportion in training data. Our comparison study further shows that repairing those invalid questions improves solver performance under matched training settings, indicating that invalid questions are contributing factor to performance degradation and motivating explicit validity feedback during self-evolution. Second, as shown in Figure 2(b), the questioner can repeatedly generate variants of the same underlying mathematical task by changing the wording, notation, or numerical parameters, and easily bypass existing repetition penalties. We observe substantial concentration in few mathematical task types in R-Zeros fifth round training data. Existing diversity controls could split questions with the same task structure into separate clusters. Because repetition penalties depend on cluster size, this fragmentation can weaken the penalty on frequently repeated tasks. These findings suggest that effective diversity control must be grounded in an understanding of what question asks and how it is solved, so that different expressions of the same task are recognized as repeated training content. Building on these insights, we introduce R-Quest, which promotes sustained self-evolution by explicitly assessing the validity of generated questions and the novelty of their underlying mathematical tasks. We first train the solver to recognize and reject invalid questions. During self-evolution, we incorporate its validity judgments into the questioners rewards to discourage invalid generation. We also assess task novelty through sampled pairwise comparisons, using the models understanding of the questions to identify repeated mathematical task structures. Together, these judgments restrict the questioners difficulty rewards to questions assessed as valid and novel. Both feedback signals are generated during subsequent self-evolution without further calls to stronger external models. Across two model families, R-Quest achieves the highest domain-average scores among evaluated methods on 12 benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and general reasoning. As shown in Figure 1, R-Quest sustains its gains over ten rounds of self-evolution, reaching its best mathematical performance in the final round and outperforming R-Zero by 17.32 points at the same iteration on Qwen3-4B-Base. After ten rounds of self-evolution, R-Quest is 5.75 points above the base model, whereas R-Zero is 11.57 points below it. These results demonstrate that assessing the validity and task novelty of self-generated questions provides practical route to sustained self-improvement.

sections.title: 2.1 BACKGROUND: THE QUESTIONER–SOLVER FRAMEWORK
sections.content: Self-evolution for mathematical reasoning commonly adopts questionersolver co-training framework. Following the R-Zero paradigm (Huang et al., 2025), both models share the same initialization and are trained alternately using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024).

sections.title: 2.2 QUESTIONING THE QUESTIONS: DIAGNOSING FAILURES IN SELF-EVOLUTION
INVALID QUESTIONS IN SOLVER TRAINING
sections.content: Self-generated questions are not always well posed. Our investigation into the collapse of RZero (Huang et al., 2025) reveals growing proportion of invalid generated questions. We randomly sample 200 questions from the question pool of each of the five R-Zero rounds and use GPT-5.6-Sol to assess their validity. Figure 3(a) shows that the valid-question rate falls from 76.5% in round one to 39.5% in round five, leaving most questions invalid. In addition, R-Zero would filter questions based on majority-voted answer agreement s(q), retaining those between 0.3 and 0.8. We find that among the retained questions, the valid question rate is further reduced, reaching 27.64% in round five. Thus, answer-consistency filtering increases the proportion of invalid questions in solver training data. To test whether invalid questions contribute to solver degradation, we compare GRPO training on matched original and repaired datasets using Qwen3-4B-Base. Each dataset contains 1,273 questions, including the same 766 valid questions. The remaining 507 questions are invalid in the original dataset and replaced by their repaired counterparts in the other. We use GPT-5.6-Sol to repair invalid questions while preserving the domain and minimizing changes in difficulty. Figure 3(b) shows comparable early performance followed by diverging trajectories: training on the repaired dataset yields final average score of 49.91 across seven mathematical benchmarks, compared with 46.54 on the original dataset. These results indicate that invalid training questions are contributing factor to solver degradation in self-evolution. Figure 4: Repeated question distribution and BLEU fragmentation in the fifth round of R-Zero. BLEU separates the illustrated mathematically equivalent questions into multiple different clusters.

sections.title: 2.2.2 REPETITION IN GENERATED QUESTIONS
sections.content: Generated questions can repeat the same mathematical task structure despite differences in wording, notation, or numerical parameters. Although R-Zero discourages repetition through BLEU-based clustering, lexical similarity may not capture repetition at the level of question types. In Figure 4, we show pair of mathematically equivalent questions in two separate BLEU clusters: they share the same sequence construction and requested computation, despite differences in wording and indexing. To quantify the prevalence of repeated question types, we use GPT-5.6-Sol to group 200 questions randomly sampled from the filtered question pool generated in R-Zeros fifth round. Questions in each group share the same mathematical task structure, and thus should be considered as repeated questions. The grouping protocol is detailed in Appendix B.3. As shown in Figure 4, the three largest question types account for 59.5% of the sample. Under the BLEU-based clustering procedure of R-Zero, the largest type of question is split into 22 clusters. Such fragmentation can weaken the repetition penalty (which is based on cluster size) on frequently repeated type. These findings motivate us to assess repetition based on the underlying task structure.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: As shown in Figure 2, R-Quest introduces two forms of feedback to support sustained self-evolution: (1) validity feedback from solver initialized to recognize and reject invalid questions; and (2) novelty feedback from the frozen base model, which compares sampled question pairs to identify repeated tasks. These signals guide questioner rewards during alternating questionersolver updates.

sections.title: 3.1 VALIDITY-AWARE SOLVER INITIALIZATION
sections.content: Our preliminary analysis in Section 2.2 examines invalid questions as contributor to performance collapse during self-evolution. We thus introduce validity-aware solver initialization to teach the solver to recognize invalid questions before self-evolution. We construct dataset by deduplicating questions from the solver training sets of five R-Zero iterations and randomly sampling an equal number from each iteration. We use GPT-5.6-Sol to annotate these questions in two stages. First, the annotator attempts to solve each question and assesses whether it is valid. Second, it independently solves only the valid questions to produce reference answers. We further review these answers and discard examples whose answers cannot be reliably verified. The dataset statistics and annotation protocol are provided in Appendix A.1 and A.2, respectively. We then train the base model with GRPO to return mathematical answer for valid question or INVALID for an invalid one. The model is instructed to attempt solution and use INVALID only when it identifies flaw in the question itself. We use the reward Rinit(q, a) = 1[a = a(q)] λ 1[a = INVALID a(q) = INVALID] , where a(q) is the reference answer for valid question and INVALID otherwise, and λ > 0 controls the penalty for rejecting valid questions to discourage excessive refusal. The full reward specification and training settings are provided in Appendix A.3. We initialize the solver with this model, bringing its ability to recognize invalid questions into the self-evolution loop.

sections.title: 3.2 QUESTION NOVELTY ASSESSMENT VIA SAMPLED PAIRWISE JUDGMENTS
sections.content: As discussed in Section 2.2, question diversity is another dimension along which self-evolution can collapse. We use the frozen base model to perform diversity judgment throughout self-evolution. Two questions are considered the same type when they share essentially the same mathematical setup and ask for the same kind of task. Changes in numerical values or wording alone do not establish new type, while belonging to the same broad mathematical field is insufficient to establish repetition. The full task specification is provided in Appendix B.1. Let denote the number of candidate questions in questioner rollout batch during GRPO training, and let pij {0, 1} indicate whether questions and are judged to be of the same type. These binary pairwise judgments define an exhaustive novelty gate, (cid:81) j=i(1 pij), which equals one only when

This reduces the total comparison cost to O(BK) and relaxes the exhaustive gate, with controlling how strongly repeated task types are suppressed. sections.title: 3.3 SELF-EVOLUTION WITH VALIDITY AND NOVELTY FEEDBACK
sections.content: Questioner Rewards. We initialize the solver with the validity-aware model from Section 3.1, bringing its ability to recognize and reject invalid questions into self-evolution. For generated question q, it is first instructed to assess validity while attempting solution and return INVALID if it identifies flaw in the question. We sample multiple responses and denote the fraction returning INVALID by u(q). We define the validity gate as gvalid(q) = 1 2 u(q). question is classified as invalid when gvalid(q) < 0, meaning that more than half of the responses return INVALID. For questions that pass this check, we switch to standard problem-solving instruction that asks for reasoning and final mathematical answer, and sample fresh set of responses. Let s(q) be the proportion of responses in the largest answer cluster. We define gnovel(q) to be 1 if passes the sampled novelty check in Section 3.2, and 0 otherwise. The questioner reward is Rquestion(q) = (cid:26)gvalid(q), gnovel(q)Runcertainty(q), gvalid(q) < 0, gvalid(q) 0, Runcertainty(q) = min{s(q), 1 s(q)}. where Runcertainty(q) is the uncertainty reward based on answer consistency. The questioner is updated with GRPO using this reward. The prompts for validity assessment and standard problem solving are provided in the Appendix Prompts A.5 and C.2, respectively. Solver Updates. The updated questioner generates candidate training questions. We first apply the same majority-vote validity check, then sample mathematical solutions for questions that pass. Consistent with R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025), we construct the training set using answer-consistency filtering and majority-vote pseudo-labels. The solver is updated with GRPO on this dataset, mixed with small, fixed proportion of the solver initialization data to maintain its ability to recognize and reject invalid questions. Replay examples retain the validity-aware task and reward defined in Appendix A.3. The questioner and solver are then updated alternately. Sampling settings, filtering thresholds, and the replay proportion are provided in Appendix C.2.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Models and Baselines. We evaluate Qwen3-4B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) and OctoThinker-3BHybrid-Base (Wang et al., 2025), covering Qwen (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024) model families. OctoThinker uses mid-training to address the limited gains from applying GRPO directly to Llama base models (Wang et al., 2025). We compare against the base models, RZero, and two recent methods for stabilizing self-evolution, OCNR (Lee et al., 2026) and R-Diverse (Li et al., 2026a). Baseline descriptions and implementation details are provided in Appendix D. Evaluation. We evaluate on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, three general-domain reasoning benchmarks, and two code generation benchmarks. In line with baselines (Huang et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026), we report mean@32 on AMC and both AIME benchmarks, and greedy-decoding accuracy on the remaining reasoning benchmarks. Code generation is evaluated on HumanEval+ (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP+ (Austin et al., 2021) using EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023), with pass@1 as the metric. For each domain, we report the checkpoint with the highest average benchmark score across evaluated rounds. Benchmark descriptions and evaluation settings are provided in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4.2 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: R-Quest outperforms self-evolution baselines in mathematical reasoning. Conin previous sistent with evaluations work (Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a), we compare all methods over five rounds of self-evolution, reporting the checkpoint with the highest mathematical average for each method. As shown in Table 1, RQuest achieves the highest average performance across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks on both backbones, surpassing R-Zero, OCNR, and R-Diverse. It improves over Qwen3-4B-Base by 5.47 points and over OctoThinker-3B by 5.79 points. Relative to R-Zero, R-Quest yields additional gains of 2.54 and 2.44 points. Across both backbones, validity-aware initialization yields mathematical performance close to that of the base models. Most of R-Quests gains emerge during subsequent self-evolution, suggesting that initialization supports later learning by enabling the solver to provide validity feedback. Measured from the same base models, R-Quest delivers 1.87 and 1.73 times the gains achieved by R-Zero, respectively, increasing the benefit of self-evolution across Qwen and Llama model families. sections.title: 4.3.2 VALIDITY ASSESSMENT DURING SELF-EVOLUTION
sections.content: Self-evolution strengthens validity assessment in R-Quest. We evaluate each rounds solver validity assessment on the same 297 questions held out from the training process, as described in Appendix A.1. Using Prompt A.5, each solver is instructed to answer valid questions and reject invalid ones, with one greedy response generated per question. We report balanced accuracy as 1 2 (Recallvalid + Recallinvalid), where the two terms are the fractions of valid questions accepted and invalid questions rejected, respectively. R-Quests balanced accuracy increases from 64.80% after initialization to 72.93% in round ten (Figure 6(a)). Since solver that accepts every question achieves 50% balanced accuracy without detecting any invalid questions, we additionally report invalid recall to assess this capability directly. Figure 6(b) shows that R-Quest achieves an invalid recall of 86.36% in round ten, whereas recall for R-Zero remains between 10.23% and 26.14% across all ten rounds. Thus, the validity assessment capability of R-Quest continues to improve through self-evolution. R-Quest generates more valid questions. We next examine whether stronger solver validity assessment is accompanied by improved question quality. For each method and round, we randomly sample 200 questions from the unfiltered pool generated by their questioner. We query GPT-5.6-Sol to assess each questions validity and compute the validity rate. Figure 6(c) shows that R-Quest increases this rate from 88.0% in round one to 94.597.5% throughout rounds four to ten. In contrast, the rate for R-Zero falls from 76.5% to 49.0%. This indicates that R-Quest steers question generation toward valid problems as self-evolution proceeds. R-Quest solver derives more reliable answers. Question generation and answer supervision are coupled across rounds: generated questions shape solver training, and the updated solver supplies pseudo-labels for subsequent rounds. Among the 200 questions sampled for each method and round, we evaluate majority-answer accuracy only on those judged valid, since invalid questions do not provide well-defined mathematical targets for solver training. We query GPT-5.6-Sol independently to derive and verify reference answers, and compare the majority-voted answers with these references. We report strict accuracy over questions with verified references, giving no credit to missing answers or unresolved judgments. Figure 6(d) shows that the two methods begin with comparable accuracy, but by round ten, R-Quest retains 54.69% accuracy, whereas R-Zero falls to just 2.06%. This shows that the deterioration in R-Zero extends from question generation to answer supervision. By maintaining predominantly valid question distribution and more reliable pseudo-labels, R-Quest preserves the quality of self-generated supervision that supports sustainable self-evolution.

sections.title: 4.3.3 QUESTION DIVERSITY DURING SELF-EVOLUTION
sections.content: R-Quest limits the concentration of recurring exercise patterns. Following the analysis in Section 2.2.2, we uniformly sample 200 solver training question records without replacement for each

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: method and round over the first five rounds. GPT-5.6-Sol sequentially groups them by their underlying mathematical construction and requested task. We measure concentration using the top-five share, the fraction of questions in the five largest groups, averaged over three random orderings of the same sample. Appendix B.3 provides the grouping procedure and task specification. As shown in Figure 7, the top-five share for R-Zero rises from 17.0% to 69.0% between rounds one and five. R-Quest with the default = 8 remains less concentrated throughout, reaching 24.0% in round five while maintaining higher performance. Overly strict diversity control can limit mathematical gains. We further examine the strength of novelty control in Figure 7 by increasing from its default value of 8 to 16, with other settings unchanged. larger increases the probability that questions from recurring exercise patterns are rejected by the novelty gate (Appendix Figure 8). This further lowers the top-five share, most notably from 30.0% to 16.8% in round four. However, performance remains below that of = 8 throughout, suggesting that overly strict diversity control may suppress more challenging variants within recurring exercise patterns. Effective novelty control should therefore balance exploration of new exercise patterns with progress toward harder problems within existing ones. sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Self-improving Reasoning Models. Label-free reinforcement learning uses model confidence, answer agreement, and entropy as training signals (Zhao et al., 2026b; Zuo et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026). Complementary work learns to generate training tasks through self-play. Absolute Zero validates tasks and solutions through code execution (Zhao et al., 2026a), while R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025) and Self-Questioning Language Models (Chen et al., 2026) train question generators and solvers using model-derived feedback. Related frameworks ground learning in games, document corpora, vision tasks, and tool environments (Liu et al., 2026; 2025; Yue et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026c;b; Li et al., 2026b; He et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Our work examines the conditions under which self-generated questions support sustained improvement, focusing on question validity and task novelty. Question Validity and Diversity in Self-evolution. For validity, prior work studies question validity in synthetic mathematical data (Liang et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). For self-evolution, VHG (Lai et al., 2026) relies on stronger external model (GPT-5.4) to verify general mathematical problems during self-play. We teach the solver to reject invalid questions through midtraining, avoiding calls to stronger external models during subsequent self-evolution. For diversity, recent methods assess novelty using distances between solver representations or code-embedding similarity (Lee et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). R-Diverse targets repetition in underlying reasoning procedures, but relies on an additional code generator (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (Hui et al., 2024)) and code encoder (Jina-Code-Embeddings-1.5B (Kryvosheieva et al., 2025)) during self-evolution. This departs from the goal of self-contained self-evolution, where the model generates its own training feedback. We instead reduce novelty assessment to an atomic judgment of whether two questions are variations of the same mathematical task, allowing frozen copy of the same base model to provide novelty feedback with only few random within-batch comparisons.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We identified invalid questions and repeated mathematical tasks as two bottlenecks to sustained self-evolution. R-Quest addresses these bottlenecks by enabling the solver to recognize and reject invalid questions and using validity and task-level novelty feedback to guide question generation. Across two model families and 12 benchmarks, R-Quest achieves the highest domain-average scores among evaluated methods in mathematics, code generation, and general reasoning. It further sustains gains over ten rounds on Qwen3-4B-Base, reaching its best mathematical performance in the final round. Further analyses show that R-Quest strengthens validity assessment, limits task repetition, and maintains more reliable majority-vote supervision across rounds. These findings highlight the ability to assess self-generated questions as key component of sustained self-improvement.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We provide the information required to reproduce the main training and evaluation pipeline in the paper and appendices. Appendix describes construction of the validity-aware initialization dataset, the annotation and reference-answer review procedures, the complete prompts, reward function, and mid-training hyperparameters. Appendix specifies the semantic novelty judgment and sampling procedure. Appendix provides the question-generation and problem-solving prompts, questionevaluation procedure, solver-data construction, replay strategy, sampling parameters, and GRPO training settings. Appendix documents the implementations and configurations of the R-Zero, OCNR, and R-Diverse baselines, and Appendix specifies the evaluation benchmarks, decoding procedures, answer judging, and reported metrics.

After deduplication within and across iterations, we randomly sample 460 questions per iteration, assigning 400 to training and 60 to validation. Annotation and answer review yield final dataset of 2,240 questions, with statistics reported in Table 4. Table 5 reports the distribution of error types among invalid questions. Both stages use only the question, without the original R-Zero pseudo-label. First, the model attempts to solve each question and assesses whether it is valid using Prompt A.1. Category is mapped to VALID, and BF to INVALID. Prompt A.1: Validity annotation You are careful reference judge for generated mathematical and reasoning questions. You see only the question. Restate its goal, inspect every definition and condition, check for contradictions and multiple reasonable interpretations, and genuinely attempt solution. Then classify: = self-contained, valid, solvable, and uniquely gradable; = meaningful but open-ended or not precisely gradable; = missing conditions, multiple answers, or key ambiguity; = contradictory or has no solution; = malformed, undefined, garbled, or unintelligible; = you cannot judge reliably. Use only when all strict requirements hold. question can have multiple solutions and still be when it explicitly asks for the complete solution set and that set is objectively gradable. Judge only the question as written. Keep the reasoning summary concise but concrete. For A, invalid_type must be null; for B-F choose the single closest invalid_type. Second, separate call independently solves the valid questions to produce reference answers using Prompt A.2. Prompt A.2: Reference answers You are the answer-verification pass for mathematical reasoning dataset. The validity pass has already classified this question as (valid). Solve it completely from scratch. Do not copy or trust an answer hint that may appear in the question. Check every stated condition, substitute or otherwise verify the result, and confirm that the final answer answers exactly what was asked.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Prompt A.2: Reference answers (continued) canonical_final_answer must be concise answer suitable for exact or mathematical-equivalence rewarding, without reasoning or boxed wrapper. Set answer_verified=true only when you have high confidence that the answer is correct and complete. If reliable verification is not possible, set it false and explain the uncertainty; never invent an answer to satisfy the schema. We then review the reference answers and exclude questions whose answers cannot be reliably verified. Prompts A.3 and A.4 provide the review instructions, with the latter used for questions requiring further review. Questions flagged for HUMAN_REVIEW were manually reviewed and retained only when their validity and reference answers could be verified; unresolved cases were excluded. Prompt A.3: Answer review You are an independent mathematical answer consistency auditor. You receive an opaque question ID, the question, Pass 1 derived answer (which may be missing), and Pass 2 canonical answer. Neither answer is authoritative. Read the question carefully and identify exactly what it asks. Independently do the mathematical checks needed to decide whether the canonical answer is correct, complete, and responsive. Decide whether an ambiguity in the question could change the answer. Compare the two supplied answers by mathematical meaning, not merely by string equality: different strings can be equivalent, and equal strings are not proof of correctness. If reliable verification is not possible, say so explicitly. Keep reasoning_summary concise and concrete; do not provide long proof. Relation meanings: - AGREE: same answer and meaning. - EQUIVALENT: different presentation but mathematically equivalent. - CONFLICT: incompatible answers. - NOT_COMPARABLE: their forms or scopes do not permit reliable direct comparison. - MISSING: the derived answer is absent. Set needs_deep_review whenever there is correctness concern, material ambiguity, conflict, or insufficient basis for high-confidence screening decision. Prompt A.4: Further answer review You are the independent deep reviewer for mathematical answer dataset. You receive only an opaque question ID, the question, prior derived answer (possibly missing), and canonical answer (possibly missing). None is authoritative. Solve the question independently from first principles. Verify what the question actually asks, whether it is clear and valid, and whether your independently derived answer is complete and responsive. Then assess the canonical answer and compare your answer separately with the derived and canonical answers by mathematical meaning, not string equality. Do not assume agreement means correctness. If ambiguity can change the answer, or reliable verification is not possible, say so. Recommend KEEP_CANONICAL only when the canonical answer is independently confirmed. Recommend REPLACE_CANONICAL only when the canonical answer is wrong or missing and your replacement is reliably verified. Recommend EXCLUDE for materially ambiguous or invalid question. Recommend HUMAN_REVIEW for unresolved conflicts or uncertainty. Keep reasoning_summary concise but include the decisive mathematical check. When recommending REPLACE_CANONICAL, set replacement_answer to exactly the independently_derived_answer; otherwise set replacement_answer to null. A.3 REWARD AND TRAINING SETTINGS We train Qwen3-4B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) and OctoThinker-3B-Hybrid-Base (Wang et al., 2025) with GRPO to return mathematical answer for valid question or INVALID for an invalid one, using Prompt A.5.

Prompt B.1: Semantic comparison You are judging whether two generated math problems are repetitions of the same recurring exercise pattern. Choose SAME_TYPE when the two problems have essentially the same distinctive mathematical setup and ask the same kind of task, so that they feel like variations of the same exercise. Do not choose SAME_TYPE merely because the problems share broad topic, similar wording, presentation style. If the common pattern is not clear and specific, choose DIFFERENT. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: helps interpret the results in Section 4.3.3, where = 16 lowers the top-five share but yields worse mathematical performance than = 8. Overly strict novelty control may suppress not only repeated exercises but also more challenging variants within the same pattern, limiting opportunities for further learning. The default budget therefore balances suppression of recurring patterns with room for continued exploration within them. B.3 EXERCISE-PATTERN CONCENTRATION ANALYSIS We analyze the sampled training records without additional filtering or deduplication. Only question text is supplied to the evaluator; method names, round indices, solver responses, and group sizes are withheld. All methods and rounds use the same evaluator and prompt. For each ordering, grouping starts with an empty inventory. Questions are processed one at time using Prompt B.2. Each existing group is represented by short pattern description and the question that established it. question either joins an existing group or establishes new group with its own description and representative. Existing descriptions and representatives remain fixed throughout the pass. Each question is assigned to exactly one group. We repeat this procedure from an empty inventory under three random orderings of the same 200 records. For each pass, we sum the sizes of the five largest groups and divide by 200, or sum all groups if fewer than five are formed. We report the mean top-five share across the three orderings. Prompt B.2: Incremental exercise-pattern grouping You are grouping mathematical questions by recurring exercise pattern. Given new question and an inventory of existing groups, assign it to an existing group or establish new one. Exercise-pattern definition Questions share pattern when they have essentially the same distinctive mathematical setup and ask for the same kind of task, making them variations of the same exercise. Differences in wording, notation, numerical values, or other local details do not by themselves establish new pattern. Changes to defining conditions or the requested task warrant separate group when they change the underlying exercise. shared broad topic or generic solution technique is not sufficient. Assignment Compare the new question with the description and representative question of each existing group. Choose the best-matching group only when the shared pattern is clear and specific, without broadening the groups definition. Otherwise, create new group and briefly describe its mathematical setup and requested task. If the inventory is empty, create new group. Classify the task as stated rather than repairing it. Apparent flaws alone are not shared exercise pattern. Output Return JSON object with the following fields: group_id: the matching group ID, or NEW. pattern: concise description for new group; otherwise, an empty string. reason: brief explanation of the match or the need for new group. Existing groups Each entry contains an ID, pattern description, and representative question. {group_inventory} New question {question}

sections.content: C SELF-EVOLUTION SETTINGS C.1 TASK SPECIFICATIONS We use the question-generation and mathematical problem-solving instructions from R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025), provided in Prompts C.1 and C.2, respectively. Validity checks use Prompt A.5, and semantic comparisons use Prompt B.1. Prompt C.1: Question generation System You are an expert competition-math problem setter. FIRST, in your private scratch-pad, think step-by-step to design brand-new, non-trivial problem. The problem could come from any field of mathematics, including but not limited to algebra, geometry, number theory, combinatorics, prealgebra, probability, statistics, and calculus. Aim for difficulty such that fewer than 30 % of advanced high-school students could solve it. Avoid re-using textbook clichés or famous contest problems. THEN, without revealing any of your private thoughts, output **exactly** the following two blocks: <question> {The full problem statement on one or more lines} </question> boxed{final_answer} Do NOT output anything elseno explanations, no extra markup. User Generate one new, challenging reasoning question now. Remember to format the output exactly as instructed. Prompt C.2: Mathematical problem solving System Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. User [Question] C.2 SAMPLING AND TRAINING SETTINGS Questioner Rewards. To evaluate each generated question, the frozen solver first produces nine validity responses. question is rejected if more than half of the outputs are INVALID. For questions that pass, we sample ten fresh mathematical solutions to compute answer consistency. These signals, together with the novelty judgment, determine the questioner reward defined in Section 3.3. Questions that fail the required output format receive reward of 1. Solver Data Construction. After updating the questioner, we generate candidate training questions and apply the same evaluation procedure: nine validity responses, followed by ten mathematical solutions for questions that pass. We retain questions with answer consistency s(q) [0.3, 0.8] and non-empty majority-vote answer, which serves as the pseudo-label. Solver Training and Replay. Replay examples are sampled from the training split of the midtraining dataset to constitute 10% of the mixed solver dataset. They retain the validity-aware task and reward from Appendix A.3. On newly generated questions, the solver uses the standard mathematical problem-solving task and the R-Zero training reward: 0.9 for agreement with the pseudo-label under mathematical equivalence checking, plus 0.1 for placing reasoning inside <think> and </think> tags followed by boxed answer. Shared Settings. For question evaluation and GRPO rollouts, we use sampling temperature of 1.0 and maximum response length of 4,096 tokens. Both the questioner and solver are trained with learning rate of 106, KL coefficient of 102, and maximum prompt length of 2,048 tokens. sections.title: D BASELINE DETAILS
sections.content: Base Models. We evaluate Qwen3-4B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) and OctoThinker-3B (Wang et al., 2025) without additional training to establish their performance before self-evolution. R-Zero. We use the released implementation of R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025), which alternates reinforcement learning updates of questioner and solver. The questioner reward combines solver uncertainty with BLEU-based penalty for within-batch repetition. Generated questions are assigned pseudo-labels through majority voting and used for subsequent solver training. OCNR. We implement OCNR (Lee et al., 2026) from its published description within the R-Zero training framework. OCNR augments the questioner reward with novelty score from one-class detector trained to distinguish questions used for solver training from questions withheld from training. Following OCNRs twofold overgeneration scheme, we generate 20,000 candidate questions per round, twice our standard budget. The detector maintains one learnable center in the solver representation space. Using values reported in the paper, we set the novelty reward coefficient to 0.3, the distance temperature τ = 0.5, and the EMA update weight α = 0.05. Question representations are obtained by mean-pooling the solvers final-layer hidden states. The detector receives one full-batch SGD update per round with learning rate of 7 103. R-Diverse. We implement R-Diverse (Li et al., 2026a) from its published description within the R-Zero training framework. It penalizes repetition based on how questions are solved, both within the current batch and across rounds. Following the published configuration, we use Qwen2.5Coder-7B (Hui et al., 2024) with greedy decoding to represent questions as solution programs and Jina-Code-Embeddings-1.5B (Kryvosheieva et al., 2025) to measure their similarity within the current batch and against earlier questions. For within-batch repetition, we retain R-Zeros average-linkage clustering with cosine-distance threshold of 0.5. Following the paper, we set the coefficients of the within-batch and cross-iteration repetition penalties to 1. The memory penalty combines maximum and mean cosine similarities with equal weights and thresholds of 0.5 and 0.25, respectively. From the second round onward, historical examples are uniformly sampled to constitute 30% of the solver training data.

sections.title: E EVALUATION BENCHMARKS
sections.content: Although our self-evolution process focuses on mathematical questions, we evaluate both mathematical reasoning and its generalization to other domains. Our evaluation covers mathematical reasoning, general-domain reasoning, and code generation. Mathematical Reasoning. We evaluate on seven benchmarks: AMC, Minerva (Lewkowycz et al., 2022), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), AIME24, and AIME25. We use Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) to judge the equivalence of model answers and reference answers. Consistent with R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025), we report mean@32 on AMC and both AIME benchmarks, and accuracy under greedy decoding on the remaining benchmarks. General Domain Reasoning. We evaluate generalization beyond mathematics on three benchmarks: MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024): Multiple-choice questions across 14 academic domains, requiring both subject knowledge and reasoning. SuperGPQA (Du et al., 2026): Graduate-level multiple-choice questions across 285 disciplines, assessing specialized knowledge and reasoning. BBEH (Kazemi et al., 2025): Challenging tasks covering logical deduction, spatial reasoning, and multi-step computation. We follow the R-Zero evaluation protocol and report exact-match accuracy under greedy decoding. Code Generation. We evaluate code generation on two Python programming benchmarks: HumanEval+ (Chen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023): Completing Python functions given their signatures and natural-language specifications. MBPP+ (Austin et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023): Generating short Python programs from natural-language descriptions of basic programming tasks. We use greedy decoding and report pass@1 on the full EvalPlus test suites.

sections.title: F ADDITIONAL RESULTS
sections.content: F.1 DETAILED ABLATION RESULTS Table 9 reports the individual benchmark scores underlying the domain averages in Table 3. Removing either validity or novelty feedback lowers performance on both code generation benchmarks and all three general reasoning benchmarks. The effects vary across mathematical benchmarks, with removing validity feedback producing the largest drop on OlympiadBench. Although individual ablations achieve higher scores on some benchmarks, the full R-Quest achieves the highest average performance in all three domains.
